summary: TRILL supports arbitrary link technologies, including point-to-point links and multi-access LANs with several switches and end stations. This document specifies how TRILL switches discover each other and form adjacencies using IS-IS.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL switches exchange Hellos to learn which neighbors they can reach and whether the link passes required checks. On a shared LAN, they also elect one switch to coordinate important link behavior.

subtitle: How TRILL switches discover neighbors, confirm links, and select a designated switch on a LAN.

tldr.problem: TRILL switches use many kinds of links, and native Ethernet frames need protection from loops while switches discover neighbors and check connectivity.
tldr.mechanism: TRILL Hellos establish adjacency states, elect a Designated RBridge on LAN links, and support MTU testing and one-hop BFD. The Designated RBridge also controls whether the LAN uses a pseudonode.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7177 obsoletes RFC 6327 and updates RFC 6325. It has been updated by RFC 7780, RFC 8139, RFC 8249, RFC 8377, and RFC 8564.

sections.title: What TRILL Adjacency Covers
sections.content:
TRILL uses IS-IS routing between switches called RBridges. End stations attach over Ethernet, while RBridges can connect using different link technologies, including point-to-point and multi-access links.

This document specifies adjacency formation and termination, Designated RBridge election on LAN links, MTU matching, one-hop Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) setup, and pseudonode use. It states that its rules take precedence over conflicting rules in the TRILL base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how TRILL switches confirm a link to a neighbor and how they coordinate on shared LAN links. Some checks also apply to point-to-point links.

sections.title: Why TRILL Uses Its Own Hello Rules
sections.content:
TRILL Hellos have three jobs: identify neighbors that can be included in the topology, elect one Designated RBridge on a LAN, and find a safe MTU for communication with each neighbor.

TRILL must also prevent multiple switches from ingressing or egressing the same native frame. A native frame has no TRILL hop count while it is outside the TRILL network, so duplicate handling can create an unprotected loop. The Designated RBridge and Appointed Forwarder mechanism helps keep that handling coordinated.

On Ethernet, TRILL data and IS-IS packets use the Designated VLAN. Hello messages are not padded, and a neighbor list can be split across TLVs when it is too large for one Hello.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL uses a single designated switch on a shared LAN to help prevent native frames from circulating in an unprotected loop. Its Hellos also check neighbor reachability and the link MTU.

sections.title: How an Adjacency Becomes Usable
sections.content:
An adjacency moves through Down, Detect, 2-Way, and Report states. Down means no entry exists. Detect means a Hello was heard but two-way reachability has not been confirmed, or it was heard outside the Designated VLAN.

2-Way means the neighbor has confirmed reachability on the Designated VLAN, but one or more enabled tests may still be pending. Report means two-way reachability and every enabled test have succeeded, so the adjacency can be included in link-state information.

Hellos, holding-timer expiry, port failure, and test results move an adjacency between states. If no MTU, BFD, or other test is enabled, the adjacency can move from 2-Way to Report immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: A neighbor first appears as detected, then confirms it can hear back. It is reported to the routing system only after the required tests succeed.

sections.title: Choosing the Designated RBridge
sections.content:
On a broadcast LAN, the local RBridge and its neighbors that are not Down are candidates for Designated RBridge. The highest priority wins. If priorities match, the election compares MAC address, then Port ID, then System ID, with larger unsigned values ranked higher.

A port enters Suspended when a higher-priority port on the same link has the same MAC address. A Suspended port accepts Hellos only to manage its suspension timer and sends no Hellos.

Changing the designated RBridge can briefly interrupt native-frame service. Changing the Designated VLAN can interrupt adjacency, so the RFC recommends avoiding unnecessary changes and using a common desired VLAN when practical.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch with the highest priority becomes the LAN's designated switch. Additional identifiers break ties, and a duplicate higher-priority MAC address causes a port to suspend.

sections.title: MTU Tests and BFD Checks
sections.content:
MTU testing checks whether a link can carry IS-IS packets at the campus MTU. The campus value is the lowest advertised originating LSP buffer size, but it cannot be less than 1,470 bytes. An adjacency that fails the campus MTU test does not enter Report, or leaves that state.

Responding to an MTU probe is mandatory, although performing the test is optional. The test runs in the Designated VLAN, and TRILL Hellos remain small for loop safety.

When both neighboring ports enable BFD, they can establish a one-hop BFD session after reaching 2-Way. If BFD begins before Report, the adjacency waits for BFD and other enabled tests to pass. A failed test moves an established adjacency back from Report.
sections.plainLanguage: MTU testing checks that a link can carry the packets needed by the campus. BFD can provide another check that a neighboring switch remains reachable.

sections.title: When the LAN Uses a Pseudonode
sections.content:
A pseudonode is a representation of a LAN in link-state information. It applies only to broadcast links, and the Designated RBridge chooses whether to use one.

When the Designated RBridge sets the bypass-pseudonode bit, each RBridge reports its Report-state adjacencies directly. Otherwise, the Designated RBridge represents the LAN pseudonode and reports the other adjacencies on its behalf. This choice changes which link-state packets are generated, not how those packets are flooded.

The RFC recommends bypassing the pseudonode unless the Designated RBridge has seen at least two simultaneous Report-state adjacencies since reboot or a management reset.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudonode lets the designated switch represent the shared LAN in routing information. The switch can bypass that representation when the link does not need it.

sections.title: Hello Contents and Security
sections.content:
On Ethernet, TRILL Hellos use multicast address 01-80-C2-00-00-41 and Ethertype 0x22F4. A Hello must use the required area and circuit settings and include link-capability information. LAN Hellos use a TRILL Neighbor TLV; point-to-point Hellos use a Three-Way Handshake TLV.

A Hello must not be sent if it exceeds 1,470 bytes, but a longer received Hello is processed normally. A receiver discards a Hello when its type does not match the port or required fields are missing or invalid.

This document clarifies the TRILL base protocol and does not change its security considerations. BFD security is addressed in the BFD support specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A TRILL Hello must match the link type and contain required fields. Invalid messages are discarded; this document does not add new security rules to TRILL.
